title: Localized quasi-finite polynomial charts and their field fibres
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $k=A/\mathfrak m$ (local means that $\mathfrak m$ is its unique maximal ideal). Let $D$ be a finite type commutative $A$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], put $E=D\otimes_Ak$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], and let $Q\subset E$ be prime, with inverse image $\mathfrak q\subset D$. Suppose $n=\dim_Q\operatorname{Spec}E$ is a finite nonnegative integer [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-kun-topological-dimension-at-point]. There exist $g\in D\setminus\mathfrak q$ and an $A$-algebra map $\alpha:A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to B=D_g$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-ring-localization-away] such that $B$ is finite type over $A$ and $\alpha$ is finite type and quasi-finite at every prime [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime]. For every field $c$ equipped with a map $A\to c$, the induced map $\alpha_c:c[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to B\otimes_Ac$ is finite type and quasi-finite at every prime, the target is finite type over $c$, and there is a canonical $c$-algebra isomorphism $B\otimes_Ac\cong(D\otimes_Ac)_{g\otimes1}$, sending $b\otimes\lambda$ to the product of the images of $b$ and $\lambda$. For $c=k$ its spectrum identifies with the basic open $D_E(g\otimes1)$; the point $Q$ corresponds to a prime $Q_g$ of $T=B\otimes_Ak$, and $\dim_{Q_g}\operatorname{Spec}T=n$. If additionally $A\subset D$ are integral domains and $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$, then $g\ne0$, $B$ is a domain containing $A$, and, writing $F=D\otimes_AK$ and $H=B\otimes_AK$, $H\cong F_{g\otimes1}$ is a nonzero domain with $\operatorname{Frac}(H)\cong\operatorname{Frac}(F)$ over $K$.

source.place: Tag 00QK (lemma-finite-type-domain-over-valuation-ring-dim-fibres), passage to a principal quasi-finite polynomial chart and the induced maps on both fibres, with localization identifications made explicit.

proof.text: Because $Q$ is proper, the map $k\to E/Q$ is injective. Hence $\mathfrak q\cap A=\mathfrak m$. The residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak m)$ is $k$: every denominator outside $\mathfrak m$ already has invertible image in $A/\mathfrak m$. Thus the fibre ring in [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra], for $R=A$, $S=D$, and prime $\mathfrak q$, is exactly $E$. Its point $\ker(E\to\kappa(\mathfrak q))$ is $Q$: by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection] the primes of $E$ correspond bijectively to the primes of $D$ over $\mathfrak m$ by inverse image, with inverse $\mathfrak q\mapsto\ker(E\to\kappa(\mathfrak q))$, and $Q$ has inverse image $\mathfrak q$. Its dimension hypothesis is the given $n$. Apply that node to obtain $g\notin\mathfrak q$ and $\alpha:A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]\to B=D_g$, of finite type and quasi-finite at every prime.

source.place: Tag 00QE (lemma-quasi-finite-over-polynomial-algebra), applied in the proof of Tag 00QK (lemma-finite-type-domain-over-valuation-ring-dim-fibres).

proof.text: Choose algebra generators $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ of $D$ over $A$. Every element of $B=D_g$ is $d/g^j$, so $d_1/1,\ldots,d_r/1,1/g$ generate $B$ over $A$. For any $A$-field $c$, these generators tensored with $1$ generate $B\otimes_Ac$ over $c$: pure tensors span the tensor product and $b\otimes\lambda=(b\otimes1)(1\otimes\lambda)$. This proves both finite type assertions directly.

source.place: Tags 00CO (definition-localization) and 00CX (lemma-tensor-product); finite-generation argument for the chart and fibres of Tag 00QK.

proof.text: Fix any $A\to c$. Set $P=A[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ and $P_c=c[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$. By [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-scalar-extension], scalar extension identifies the polynomial source with $P_c$. Define $P_c\to B\otimes_Ac$ by $t_i\mapsto\alpha(t_i)\otimes1$ and $\lambda\mapsto1\otimes\lambda$; the polynomial universal property gives this map and its agreement with the scalar extension $\alpha_c$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-quasi-finite-four-rings] with $R=P$, $S=B$, $R'=P_c$, and $S'=B\otimes_Ac$. Its square commutes on coefficients and variables. Every pure tensor is the product of an image from $B$ and the image of a constant from $P_c$, and such tensors span $S'$, so its generation hypothesis holds. At each prime of $S'$, the contracted prime of $B$ satisfies the hypothesis by step 1. The node gives finite type and quasi-finiteness of $\alpha_c$ at every prime.

source.place: Tag 00PN (lemma-four-rings), used for the field-fibre maps in Tag 00QK.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-localization-away-base-change] with base $A$, algebra $D$, second algebra $c$, and element $g$. It gives the canonical $c$-algebra isomorphism $B\otimes_Ac\simeq(D\otimes_Ac)_{g\otimes1}$ with formula $(d/g^j)\otimes\lambda\mapsto(d\otimes\lambda)/(g\otimes1)^j$. Since every $b\in B$ has this fraction form, it is precisely the formula in the statement: multiply the image of $b$ by the image of $\lambda$.

For $c=k$, write $\bar g=g\otimes1$. Since $\mathfrak q$ is the inverse image of $Q$, $g\notin\mathfrak q$ implies $\bar g\notin Q$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-localization-spectrum-embedding] to $E$ and the powers of $\bar g$, and use step 4. It identifies $\operatorname{Spec}T$ with the basic open $D_E(\bar g)$ and gives the unique prime $Q_g$ above $Q$. This is an open neighbourhood of $Q$. By [lem-weil-pbc-dimension-at-point-open-subspace], its dimension at $Q$ is the dimension of $\operatorname{Spec}E$ at $Q$, namely $n$. A homeomorphism identifies open neighbourhoods and chains of irreducible closed subsets, hence preserves this dimension. Therefore $\dim_{Q_g}\operatorname{Spec}T=n$.

source.place: Tag 00CM (section-localization), fraction equality; Tag 00DK (lemma-tensor-localization), generic fibre of Tag 00QK.

proof.text: Put $u=g\otimes1\in F$, so $u\ne0$ and $H\simeq F_u$. The fraction relation makes $F\to F_u$ injective. The inclusion $F\to\operatorname{Frac}(F)$ sends $u$ to a unit, so [lem-weil-pbc-ring-localization-universal-property] extends it to $F_u\to\operatorname{Frac}(F)$ by $x/u^i\mapsto x/u^i$. This is injective since a zero fraction has zero numerator. For any injective map $f$ from a domain to a field, the formula $a/b\mapsto f(a)/f(b)$ extends it to the fraction field: cross-multiplication verifies well-definedness, and denominators remain nonzero. Apply this formula to obtain $\operatorname{Frac}(F_u)\to\operatorname{Frac}(F)$ and, conversely, $\operatorname{Frac}(F)\to\operatorname{Frac}(F_u)$ from $F\hookrightarrow F_u$. They are inverse: on $x/y$ and on $(x/u^i)/(y/u^j)$ their composites return the original fraction. Both fix $K$ because they extend the structural maps from $F$. Transporting along step 4 gives $\operatorname{Frac}(H)\simeq\operatorname{Frac}(F)$ over $K$.
